title: Little change in a changing landscape: Tracking exposure to untrustworthy news in Germany from 2017 to 2024.
screen_reason: Two waves of passive web-tracking data linked to surveys in Germany (YouGov Pulse / Wakoopa): 1,212 participants tracked for 6 months in 2017 (56 million visits) and 436 participants tracked for 2 months in 2024 (6 million visits). Domains are classified with NewsGuard (untrustworthy = score below 60). The paper reports both the share of participants who ever visited an untrustworthy news site (REACH: 17% in 2017, 9% in 2024) and the share of news visits going to untrustworthy outlets (EXPOSURE diet share: 0.75% in 2017, 0.52% in 2024), each with confidence intervals - behavioural prevalence estimates with explicit denominators.

estimates.platform: Web browsing (desktop only in 2017), passively metered; social media feed content not captured
estimates.date: 1 July 2017 to 9 December 2017 (6-month tracking window, reported as 07/17-12/17)
estimates.measure_type: % of tracked German participants who visited at least one untrustworthy news site during the tracking period
estimates.value_raw: 17% (15%-19%); 'During the longer 2017 tracking window, 17% of participants visited at least one untrustworthy news site'
estimates.denominator: 1,212 tracked German adults (YouGov Pulse online access panel, quota-matched to the online population on age, gender and education), 56 million website visits
estimates.definition: Participant recorded at least one visit to a domain rated untrustworthy by NewsGuard (score below 60) during the 6-month window
estimates.misinfo_def: "Sources are considered untrustworthy if the score is below 60 on a 0-100 scale" (NewsGuard, "an established database for source-based news credibility labels rated according to apolitical journalistic standards")
estimates.source_quote: During the longer 2017 tracking window, 17% of participants visited at least one untrustworthy news site, compared to just 8% in the shorter 2024 period.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 2; the Figure 1A sample-metadata table gives the same value with its interval: '2017 6 months (07/17-12/17) 1,212 56 million 1.6% 17% (15%-19%) 0.75% (0.50%-1.01%) 96.18 (95.91- 96.46)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard source-level credibility ratings (0-100, untrustworthy below 60); 411 unique German news domains covered; NewsGuard reports covering websites responsible for 95% of news-related social media traffic. Robustness checks at thresholds of 50 and 70 and excluding bild.de. Portal domains counted only via their news subdomains (e.g. t-online.de/nachrichten).
estimates.notes: The authors themselves warn this binary indicator is 'highly sensitive to the duration of the tracking period' (6 months in 2017 vs 2 months in 2024), so the 17% vs 9% gap is not a clean over-time comparison. Desktop-only tracking in this wave. Social media feeds are not observed, which the authors say makes these figures understate exposure (they cite up to 10x higher shares in feeds).

estimates.platform: Web browsing (desktop only in 2017), passively metered
estimates.measure_type: % of all news website visits that went to untrustworthy news outlets (user-level mean share of the news diet)
estimates.denominator: All news visits by 1,212 tracked German adults; news accounted for 1.6% of 56 million recorded URL visits
estimates.definition: Visits to domains rated untrustworthy by NewsGuard (score below 60), as a share of all NewsGuard-labelled news visits, computed per user and averaged
estimates.misinfo_def: "Sources are considered untrustworthy if the score is below 60 on a 0-100 scale" (NewsGuard)
estimates.n: 1,212 participants' news visits (news = 1.6% of 56 million URL visits)
estimates.source_quote: the share of visits to untrustworthy news outlets among all news visits—0.75% in 2017 and 0.52% in 2024—and the average NewsGuard score (ranging from 0—lowest to 100—highest reliability) across all news visits, stable at 96 in both years.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 2; Figure 1A gives the interval: '1,212 56 million 1.6% 17% (15%-19%) 0.75% (0.50%-1.01%)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard source-level credibility ratings (untrustworthy below 60); 411 German news domains; results robust to thresholds of 50 and 70, to excluding bild.de, and to minimum visit durations of 3s, 30s and 120s (raw visits reported).
estimates.notes: Denominator is NEWS visits, not all browsing; as a share of total browsing the figure would be roughly 0.012% (0.75% of 1.6%), but that is not stated and is not kept. This is a user-level mean share (individual-level measure averaged over participants), not a pooled visit count, as the CI in Figure 1A confirms.

estimates.platform: Web browsing (desktop and mobile), passively metered; social media feed content not captured
estimates.date: 4 November 2024 to 31 December 2024 (2-month tracking window, reported as 11/24-12/24)
estimates.measure_type: % of tracked German participants who visited at least one untrustworthy news site during the tracking period
estimates.value_raw: 9% (6%-11%) in the Figure 1A table; the narrative text says 'just 8% in the shorter 2024 period'
estimates.denominator: 436 tracked German adults (YouGov Pulse tracking panel, survey fielded to the whole panel without quota matching), 6 million website visits
estimates.definition: Participant recorded at least one visit to a domain rated untrustworthy by NewsGuard (score below 60) during the 2-month window
estimates.misinfo_def: "Sources are considered untrustworthy if the score is below 60 on a 0-100 scale" (NewsGuard)
estimates.page_loc: Figure 1A sample-metadata table (2024 row: tracking period 2 months, 11/24-12/24). The running text on p. 2 instead says 'compared to just 8% in the shorter 2024 period'.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard source-level credibility ratings (untrustworthy below 60); 411 German news domains; robust to thresholds of 50 and 70 and to excluding bild.de. Visits to the 12 domains used in an embedded media-literacy experiment were removed for the survey windows (removing >99% of experimental URL visits); none of them was among the top three untrustworthy domains.
estimates.moderator_quote: The second dataset, collected in 2024, spans 2 months and includes behavioral data from 436 individuals.
estimates.notes: borderline=true because the paper gives two different numbers for the same quantity: 9% (6%-11%) in the Figure 1A table and 8% in the running text. The table value is used here since it carries the CI. Two-month window (vs six months in 2017) mechanically depresses an 'ever visited' indicator, as the authors note. The 2024 sample also underrepresents far-right (AfD) voters and was collected inside a media-literacy intervention study, and the authors conclude their estimates 'likely understate actual levels of exposure'.

estimates.platform: Web browsing (desktop and mobile), passively metered
estimates.measure_type: % of all news website visits that went to untrustworthy news outlets (user-level mean share of the news diet)
estimates.denominator: All news visits by 436 tracked German adults; news accounted for 2.5% of 6 million recorded URL visits
estimates.definition: Visits to domains rated untrustworthy by NewsGuard (score below 60), as a share of all NewsGuard-labelled news visits, computed per user and averaged
estimates.misinfo_def: "Sources are considered untrustworthy if the score is below 60 on a 0-100 scale" (NewsGuard)
estimates.n: 436 participants' news visits (news = 2.5% of 6 million URL visits)
estimates.source_quote: the share of visits to untrustworthy news outlets among all news visits—0.75% in 2017 and 0.52% in 2024—and the average NewsGuard score (ranging from 0—lowest to 100—highest reliability) across all news visits, stable at 96 in both years.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 2; Figure 1A gives the interval: '436 6 million 2.5% 9% (6%-11%) 0.52% (0.19%-0.85%)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard source-level credibility ratings (untrustworthy below 60); results robust to alternative thresholds (50, 70), to excluding bild.de and to 3s/30s/120s minimum visit durations.
estimates.moderator_quote: The second dataset, collected in 2024, spans 2 months and includes behavioral data from 436 individuals. Within this sample, news websites accounted for 2.5% of recorded URLs.
estimates.notes: After 1:1 propensity-score matching (866 participants) the authors find no significant change in this share between 2017 and 2024, but a significant ~1% decline in the average NewsGuard diet-quality score. The matched-sample comparison yields regression coefficients, not a new prevalence share, so it is not rowed.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) CONCENTRATION not extracted, because R1 cannot be satisfied: 'the top three domains classified as untrustworthy (NewsGuard score below 60), including rt.de (RT, formerly Russia Today), made up 49% of visits to untrustworthy news' in 2017, and in 2024 'nius.de, reitschuster.de, and politikversagen.net—account for 23% of visits to untrustworthy news'. conc_share_pct is given (49% and 23%, source-level, exposure dimension) but conc_group_pct is not derivable: the paper never states how many untrustworthy domains were visited or exist in the German NewsGuard set (411 is ALL German news domains, trustworthy and untrustworthy together). A bare 'top three' is unusable per R1. The parallel trustworthy-side figures (top three trustworthy domains = 29% of trustworthy news visits in 2017, 32% in 2024) have the same problem and are not misinformation concentration anyway. 2) Mean NewsGuard news-diet quality scores (96.18 [95.91-96.46] in 2017; 95.76 [95.35-96.17] in 2024) are scale scores, not shares - no row. 3) The overall news share of browsing (1.6% in 2017, 2.5% in 2024) is news, not misinformation. 4) Figure 1B reports predicted group means of the untrustworthy share by demographic and political subgroup (gender, age, education, income, political interest, satisfaction with democracy, orientation, party vote, roughly 0-3%); these are subgroup model predictions read off a figure with no printed values, so nothing is extractable, though the paper's headline subgroup claim is that AfD voters had significantly higher exposure in 2017. 5) Both waves are kept as separate rows (different samples, 7 years apart, different tracking lengths); if only one Germany estimate is wanted, 2017 is the larger and better quota-matched sample and 2024 is the more current.

rob.design: Two cross-sectional passive web-tracking samples linked to surveys, collected by YouGov with Wakoopa metering. 2017: non-probability online access panel quota-matched to the online population on age, gender and education; N = 1,212; 1 July - 9 December 2017; 56 million visits; desktop only; AfD share 13.9% vs 12.6% in the federal election. 2024: survey fielded to the entire tracking panel with no quota matching; N = 436; 4 November - 31 December 2024; 6 million visits; desktop and mobile; AfD share 16.1% vs 20.8% in the 2025 federal election (underrepresented). Classification: NewsGuard domain-level credibility scores, untrustworthy below 60, 411 German news domains, portal domains counted only via news subdomains; robustness to thresholds 50/70, to excluding bild.de, and to 3s/30s/120s dwell-time cut-offs. The 2024 data come from inside a media-literacy intervention study; visits to the 12 experimental domains during survey windows (+6h) were removed, clearing >99% of experimental URL visits. Over-time comparison via 1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity-score matching on age, gender, education, political interest and non-news browsing (MatchIt), matched N = 866. No response rates reported; no article- or claim-level validation (the authors flag that outlet-level scores cannot capture within-source variation, and that social media feeds are unobserved).
rob.item6_quote: Following best practice for source-based research on misinformation and news trustworthiness (Lin et al., 2023; Lühring et al., 2024), we used NewsGuard—an established database for source-based news credibility labels rated according to apolitical journalistic standards—to classify websites as trustworthy or untrustworthy. ... Sources are considered untrustworthy if the score is below 60 on a 0–100 scale.
rob.item10_quote: During the longer 2017 tracking window, 17% of participants visited at least one untrustworthy news site, compared to just 8% in the shorter 2024 period. ... We therefore focus on two alternative individual-level measures: the share of visits to untrustworthy news outlets among all news visits—0.75% in 2017 and 0.52% in 2024
